text: Engineering Education: A Multi-Course Assessment Across Bloom’s Taxonomy Ghazal Barari 1, Debarati Basu 2,Y uetong Lin1, (Senior Member, IEEE), and Jorge Ortega-Moody1, (Member, IEEE) 1School of Engineering, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University Worldwide, Daytona Beach, FL, 32114 USA 2Department of Engineering Fundamentals, College of Engineering, Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, FL, 32114 USA Corresponding author: Ghazal Barari (e-mail: bararig@erau.edu) ABSTRACTLarge language models (LLMs) such as GPT-5, Claude, and Grok are increasingly incorporated into engineering education, yet their effectiveness on discipline-specific cognitive tasks remains insufficiently characterized. Engineering learning relies heavily on conceptual understanding, multi-step problem solving, and higher-order reasoning, making it essential to evaluate how LLMs perform across these contexts. This study investigates the performance of three LLMs across four undergraduate engineering courses,Thermodynamics,Computer Programming,Systems and Control, and Circuits, using multiple-choice questions aligned with Bloom’s Taxonomy. We examine differences in accuracy and reasoning quality across cognitive levels, compare zero-shot and context-assisted prompting, and benchmark LLM performance against human learners inComputer Programming. Forty-eight instructor-designed questions (12 per course) spanning all Bloom levels were administered to each model. Responses were evaluated using accuracy, a rubric-based reasoning score, and a Composite Performance Index capturing completeness, efficiency, and quality of support. Human performance data were collected through an IRB-approved assessment with undergraduate students. Results show that Claude demonstrated the strongest overall performance and consistency, GPT-5 excelled in analytical reasoning, and Grok exhibited variable accuracy with limited higher-order reasoning.

Providing contextual information improved GPT-5’s performance but had minimal impact on Claude or Grok. In Programming, Claude and GPT-5 outperformed human participants across all Bloom levels. These findings suggest that LLMs can support engineering learning when paired with instructional strategies emphasizing verification and critical evaluation. However, persistent limitations at higher cognitive levels highlight the importance of guided, responsible integration, supported by a practical instructional guide for effective LLM use across engineering tasks. INTRODUCTION T HE emergence of large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-5, Claude, and Grok has transformed the landscape of education by introducing new possibilities for content generation, tutoring support, and automated reasoning [1]. While these models have demonstrated strong performance on general knowledge assessments, their ef- fectiveness in domain-specific, technical fields such as en- gineering remains less thoroughly understood [2]. Engi- neering education demands not only factual recall but also conceptual understanding, applied problem-solving, and the interpretation of quantitative data, skills that may challenge even the most advanced AI systems. Understanding how AI models perform under these con- ditions not only informs their current utility as educational tools but also sheds light on their limitations as reasoning agents in engineering contexts. The findings can help guide both instructional design and responsible integration of AI into engineering curricula while minimizing the challenges associated with AI in education [3], [4]. Recent research focus on evaluating AI across Bloom’s taxonomy levels [11] aligns with pedagogical goal by highlighting the varying cognitive demands where AI currently excels or struggles, thereby informing targeted educational interven- tions [12], [13]. A. LITERATURE REVIEW 1) Generative AI (GAI) and Engineering Education Artificial intelligence (AI), and more recently generative ar- tificial intelligence (GAI), is increasingly shaping research, teaching, and professional practices in engineering educa- tion.

AI-based systems are becoming embedded in engineer- ing workflows and educational environments, augmenting human cognitive and professional practices through algo- rithmic systems that assist with tasks such as information re- trieval, design exploration, and data analysis. As Johri notes, AI-driven tools extend human cognition by redistributing aspects of reasoning and problem solving across human - machine systems, enabling engineers and learners to manage increasing levels of complexity in technical work [14]. Recent advances in GAI, particularly systems built on foundational models such as large language models (LLMs) have further expanded these capabilities by allowing users to generate explanations, code, design ideas, and analytical responses through natural language interaction. In educa- tional contexts, these systems offer opportunities to support both instructional practices and self-directed learning by providing on-demand explanations, examples, and problem- solving assistance. At the same time, the integration of GAI into engineering education raises important pedagogical and ethical consid- erations. Because these systems generate responses based on probabilistic patterns in training data rather than true semantic understanding, their outputs may contain inaccu- racies, biases, or misleading information [15]. Consequently, literature emphasizes the importance of cultivating critical AI literacy among engineering students so that they can interpret, evaluate, and responsibly use AI-generated out- puts. As the adoption of GAI tools continues to expand, systematic evaluation of their capabilities and limitations within authentic engineering learning contexts becomes essential.

As the adoption of GAI tools continues to expand, systematic evaluation of their capabilities and limitations within authentic engineering learning contexts becomes essential. In particular, understanding how LLMs perform on engineering tasks of varying cognitive complexity and how their responses compare with human reasoning can inform responsible pedagogical integration of AI tools in engineering curricula. 2) Evaluations of LLM Performance in STEM Contexts Recent empirical studies have begun to systematically eval- uate the performance of large language models (LLMs) on academic assessments and domain-specific tasks. For example, Kunget al.[16] examined ChatGPT’s performance on the United States Medical Licensing Examination, while Friederet al.[17] evaluated the mathematical capabilities of ChatGPT (two versions) and GPT-4 using newly created datasets that focus on advanced mathematical reasoning tasks. Within STEM education, emerging research has also explored how LLMs perform on structured scientific and engineering problem-solving tasks. For instance, Wanget al.investigated ChatGPT’s ability to solve problems from a college-level engineering physics course, including both well-specified textbook-style problems and under-specified real-world problems. Their findings showed that ChatGPT successfully solved approximately 62.5% of well-specified problems but only 8.3% of open-ended problems, high- lighting substantial limitations when tasks required mod- eling real-world situations or making assumptions about missing information [18].

Analysis of incorrect solutions further revealed several failure modes, including difficulties constructing accurate models of physical systems, gener- ating reasonable assumptions when data were incomplete, and performing reliable numerical calculations.These results suggest that while LLMs can effectively retrieve and apply known formulas or concepts in well-structured scenarios, their reasoning performance becomes less reliable in more open-ended problem-solving contexts. A recent work has also examined LLMs as conversational AI tutors in engi- neering and computer science education [19]. They eval- uated several LLMs, including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Meta AI—on an open-ended computer architecture question using metrics such as accuracy, persuasiveness, and depth of explanation. Their results show that although mod- els often produced largely accurate responses, the quality of explanations varied across systems, highlighting the impor- tance of evaluating LLMs that assess not only correctness but also the quality of AI-generated responses. Within engineering education specifically, studies have also begun to examine the pedagogical integration of gen- erative AI tools. For example, El Fathiet al.[20] explored the use of ChatGPT as a supplemental instructional tool in an introductory thermodynamics course and reported im- provements in conceptual understanding within an inquiry- based learning environment. At the same time, scholars have raised concerns regarding the reliability of LLM outputs in structured analytical or high-stakes problem-solving set- tings [21]. In technical domains such as engineering, hallucinations can lead to erroneous conclusions or unsafe recommendations if not carefully scrutinized. This inherent uncertainty shows the importance of not treating AI outputs as infallible but rather as starting points for critical analysis and validation [25]. In another study, Fulsher,et al.[26] reviewed how gen- erative AI can both generate and correct misinformation within educational contexts. Their analysis shows that most research focuses on identifying individual student miscon- ceptions, with less attention to community- and system- level misinformation risks. As AI tools become increasingly accessible, their integra- tion into engineering education offers exciting opportunities for enhancing student learning and engagement. However, encouraging responsible and reflective use of AI is critical to ensure that students develop the skills to critically evaluate AI outputs rather than passively accepting them [27], [28]. This study provides a framework to support such engage- ment by highlighting the varying capabilities and limitations of AI models when applied to engineering problems across multiple cognitive levels. 4) Bloom’s Revised T axonomy as a Evaluation Framework Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy provides a widely used frame- work for designing and evaluating educational assess- ments by categorizing cognitive processes into hierarchical levels—remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating [29], [30]. In engineering educa- tion, Bloom-aligned learning objectives are frequently used to structure course assessments so that students progres- sively develop conceptual understanding, analytical reason- ing, and problem-solving abilities. As a result, Bloom’s taxonomy plays an important role not only in curriculum development but also in the design of assessment tasks that measure different levels of cognitive engagement [31], [32]. Despite its extensive use in educational assessment de- sign, Bloom’s taxonomy has only recently begun to be explored as a framework for evaluating the capabilities of LLMs.

Despite its extensive use in educational assessment de- sign, Bloom’s taxonomy has only recently begun to be explored as a framework for evaluating the capabilities of LLMs. In LLM research, model performance is commonly assessed using benchmarks, which are standardized datasets of tasks designed to evaluate capabilities such as language understanding, reasoning, or mathematical problem solving. However, benchmark evaluations typically report aggregate accuracy without distinguishing the cognitive processes re- quired by different tasks. Recent work has begun to address this limitation by mapping benchmark tasks to Bloom’s taxonomy and analyzing the cognitive levels represented in widely used LLM evaluation datasets [33]. These analyses show that many benchmarks predominantly assess lower and mid-level cognitive skills such as remembering, under- standing, and applying, while higher-order reasoning tasks remain underrepresented. Another study evaluated GPT4 on 307 psychosomatic medicine multiple-choice exam ques- tions and reported high overall performance. Using Bloom’s taxonomy to qualitatively analyze incorrect responses, they found that errors occurred primarily at the remembering and understanding levels, with additional failures in applying concepts to new situations [34]. In addition, recent work on AI-supported learning environments proposes Bloom- informed prompt design strategies to scaffold higher-order thinking when interacting with LLMs [35]. Together, these studies suggest that Bloom’s taxonomy provides a useful cognitive and evaluation framework for analyzing how LLMs perform across different types of tasks.

Building on these literature, the present study applies a Bloom-aligned evaluation framework to engineering educa- tion contexts, evaluating LLM performance on questions designed to represent multiple cognitive levels across un- dergraduate engineering courses. 5) Pedagogical Implications of AI-Supported Learning Evaluating AI performance on Bloom-aligned tasks can also provide insights into how AI tools may complement human learning processes. For example, comparing model responses under different instructional conditions, such as with and without contextual guidance, can reveal how AI systems respond to varying levels of scaffolding [36]. Such analyses may encourage students to view AI not merely as a source of answers but as a collaborative tool that requires critical interpretation and verification [37]. Exposure to AI-generated reasoning including both cor- rect and flawed responses can also foster metacognitive awareness, encouraging students to question assumptions, cross-check information, and reflect on their problem- solving strategies [9], [38]. Consequently, responsible inte- gration of AI tools into engineering education may support active learning, critical thinking, and ethical technology use [39], [40]. Preparing students for a future where hu- man–AI collaboration is common therefore requires instruc- tional approaches that emphasize both effective AI use and professional judgment [41]. As discussed earlier, benchmark-based evaluations often treat cognitive complexity implicitly, rather than explicitly op- erationalizing the type of reasoning required by a task. Al- though recent studies have begun to map benchmark datasets to Bloom’s taxonomy, these analyses suggest that exist- ing benchmarks disproportionately assess lower- and mid- level cognitive processes, leaving higher-order reasoning tasks comparatively underrepresented. Furthermore, prior evaluations rarely distinguish between task difficulty and cognitive operation, making it difficult to determine whether reported performance reflects genuine reasoning capabilities or pattern-based answer generation. These methodological limitations highlight the need for structured, cognitively differentiated evaluation frameworks, particularly within au- thentic engineering education contexts. To address these gaps, the present study adopts a multi- course, Bloom-aligned evaluation framework to examine LLM performance on questions spanning multiple cogni- tive levels in undergraduate engineering courses. Unlike prior studies that rely primarily on single-discipline bench- marks or accuracy-only metrics, this approach combines correctness-based evaluation with rubric-guided analysis of reasoning quality, allowing differentiation between surface- level answer selection and deeper explanatory reasoning across cognitive categories.

In addition, by examining model responses under different instructional conditions and com- paring them with human student performance, this study provides contextual grounding for interpreting LLM capa- bilities in educational settings. However, this study shares limitations common in ex- ploratory LLM evaluation research, including a finite instructor-designed item bank and reliance on descriptive statistics. These constraints are acknowledged and frame the findings as methodological illustration rather than definitive validation. B. RESEARCH PROBLEM AND KNOWLEDGE GAP Despite growing empirical studies evaluating LLMs in edu- cation, existing work primarily reports descriptive accuracy metrics on isolated tasks or standardized benchmarks. Few studies systematically examine LLM performance across multiple engineering domains while explicitly differentiat- ing cognitive task types using a validated learning taxonomy. Furthermore, prior research rarely distinguishes whether observed performance differences reflect task difficulty, prompt design, or underlying cognitive operations. To address this gap, this study investigates how Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy can serve as a structured analytical framework for examining LLM performance across distinct engineering domains. This work is guided by the following research questions: RQ1: How do LLMs perform across different cognitive levels defined by Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy in undergrad- uate engineering courses? RQ2: Do LLMs exhibit consistent strengths or weak- nesses across engineering domains when tasks are aligned with cognitive levels? RQ3: How does the availability of instructional context influence LLM performance across cognitive categories? RQ4: How does LLM performance compare with human learners under controlled conditions when evaluated using Bloom-aligned tasks?

RQ4: How does LLM performance compare with human learners under controlled conditions when evaluated using Bloom-aligned tasks? This study positions its contribution as methodological (a structured Bloom-aligned evaluation framework), empirical (cross-course comparative findings), and conceptual (analy- sis of LLM reasoning patterns through a cognitive lens). C. RESEARCH OBJECTIVES This study evaluates LLMs across four engineering courses: Thermodynamics, Computer Programming, Systems and Control and Circuits for Engineering Technology. For each course, we developed 12 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) that span all six levels of Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy, from remembering and understanding to analyzing and creating. These questions were designed not to replicate textbook problems, but to assess a model’s ability to interpret, reason, and apply knowledge in a pedagogically meaningful way. Importantly, we compare AI performance under two distinct conditions: 1) without any instructional context (zero-shot inference), and 2) with access to curated reference material, simulating the kind of support a student might receive during open-resource learning. We will also compare the LLMs performance with human inComputer Programming to evaluate how closely these models align with typical student outcomes and where meaningful gaps in reasoning or accuracy remain. By applying a structured and comparative approach, this study contributes to the growing body of research on AI in education with three key objectives: 1) To measure the accuracy and reasoning quality of LLMs across a range of engineering domains. 2) To assess whether LLMs exhibit consistent strengths or weaknesses across different levels of cognitive com- plexity. 3) To evaluate how the presence of instructional material affects AI performance on discipline-specific problem sets.

The two-condition approach, contrasting zero-shot and context-assisted scenarios, also investigates whether provid- ing curated instructional content can reduce the likelihood of hallucinations and improve reasoning fidelity. Under- standing these dynamics will help educators and students recognize when and how to appropriately leverage AI tools. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. METHODOLOGY This study employs a structured, comparative, and cross- sectional design to evaluate the performance of large lan- guage models (LLMs) on engineering problem-solving tasks across four undergraduate engineering courses:Thermody- namics,Computer Programming,Systems and Controland Circuitsfor Engineering Technology. The evaluation focuses on two distinct testing conditions: 1) Zero-shot inference (without content): LLMs answer questions without access to instructional or reference material. 2) Context-assisted inference (with content): LLMs are provided with carefully curated reference content re- lated to each course before answering. Each model was evaluated on a common set of 12 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) per course, designed to represent a broad range of cognitive tasks defined by Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. The experimental procedure is summarized in Fig. 1, which illustrates the two testing conditions as well as the evaluation workflow for assessing accuracy and reasoning quality across the four courses. A. QUESTION DEVELOPMENT A total of 48 MCQs were developed, 12 for each course, by a team of instructors with domain expertise. These questions were not directly taken from textbooks, but rather designed to evaluate students’ understanding, application, and rea- soning abilities based on common engineering principles.

These questions were not directly taken from textbooks, but rather designed to evaluate students’ understanding, application, and rea- soning abilities based on common engineering principles. Each question was categorized into one of the six Bloom’s cognitive levels as shown in Table I. To enhance methodological transparency and replicability, each question was classified into a Bloom cognitive level using explicit operational criteria derived from Krathwohl’s revision of Bloom’s taxonomy. Rather than relying solely on instructor labeling, classification was guided by the primary cognitive operation required to correctly solve the task. Questions were reviewed independently by two instruc- tors with domain expertise to ensure alignment between the dominant cognitive operation and assigned Bloom category. Disagreements were resolved through discussion to achieve consensus classification. This operationalization approach reduces reliance on subjective labeling and clarifies how cognitive distinctions were applied in task design. Although multiple-choice questions are traditionally as- sociated with lower-order assessment, prior assessment re- search demonstrates that well-designed MCQs can capture higher-order cognitive processes when distractors require evaluation of assumptions, synthesis of relationships, and judgment of alternatives. In this study, Evaluate and Create- level items were structured to require comparative reasoning and justification rather than simple recall. REFERENCE MATERIAL FOR CONTEXT -ASSISTED RUNS ForThermodynamics, a concise reference packet was pre- pared to simulate instructional material available to stu- dents during open-book or guided learning situations. These packets contained key definitions and equations; Sample problem summaries (2-3 worked-out examples); Excerpts from thermodynamic or engineering property tables (where applicable); Process diagrams or schematics For theComputer Programmingcourse, the lecture mate- rial relevant to each question was provided to the LLMs. All content was consolidated into a single file that in- cluded: Explanations of the underlying concepts; Simple code demonstrations or examples; Illustrations of common errors associated with the concept; and Flowcharts depicting the logic or process related to the topic. This material was fed into the model as context prior to question presentation during the context-assisted condition. C. AI MODELS EVALUATED Three prominent LLMs were evaluated: •ChatGPT (GPT-5, OpenAI) •Claude (Anthropic) •Grok (xAI) Each model was tested under both conditions (zero-shot and context-assisted) across all four courses. The same prompts and input structure were used for all models to ensure consistency. All models were accessed through their publicly available interfaces using default system configu- rations at the time of testing. Decoding parameters such as temperature, top-p, maximum tokens, and random seed were not manually modified. Each question was presented once per condition (zero-shot and context-assisted), and responses were recorded without multiple stochastic runs or aggregation procedures. DATA ANAL YSIS Data were analyzed using a combination of descriptive and comparative statistical methods to examine LLM perfor- mance across courses and cognitive levels. Descriptive anal- ysis focused on accuracy frequency, percentage of correct responses, and score distribution across cognitive levels, while comparative analyses provided insights into differ- ences across models, courses, and Bloom’s taxonomy levels. The data analysis examined multiple dimensions of LLM performance to provide both quantitative and qualitative in- sights. Overall accuracy and average reasoning scores were calculated for each course, model, and testing condition to establish baseline performance patterns. To further explore cognitive variability, scores were distributed across Bloom’s taxonomy levels,i.e.remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating, to identify where each model demonstrated strength or limitation. COMPOSITE PERFORMANCE INDEX (CPI) To evaluate and compare the overall performance of the three LLMs, a Composite Performance Index (CPI) was de- veloped. The CPI provides a single, normalized measure of each model’s effectiveness based on four key dimensions of response quality: Accuracy, Completeness, Efficiency, and Support. Higher CPI scores correspond to better-performing LLM outputs across the evaluated criteria. Accuracy (A)measures whether the model produced the correct final answer on the first attempt.

Higher CPI scores correspond to better-performing LLM outputs across the evaluated criteria. Accuracy (A)measures whether the model produced the correct final answer on the first attempt. It was assigned a binary value: 1 if the initial response was correct, and 0 if incorrect. Completeness (C)reflects the degree to which the re- sponse contained all necessary reasoning steps, explana- tions, and contextual detail. It was rated using a rubric score (1-5) and normalized by dividing the score by 5 to yield a value between 0 and 1. Efficiency (E)captures how quickly and concisely the model reached a complete answer. This was quantified using the number of follow-up prompts required to achieve a correct and complete response, expressed as given in Eq. (1): E= 1 1 +N f (1) whereN f is the number of follow-up questions. Thus, a model that produced a complete answer without follow- ups received an efficiency score of1. The efficiency metric reflects conversational compactness (number of follow-up prompts) rather than pedagogical quality and should not be interpreted as implying that fewer interactions are inherently more educationally effective. Support (S)represents the model’s ability to enrich its response through the use of visual examples, contextual expansion, or additional explanatory depth. A value of1 was assigned if such support was present and0otherwise. Each dimension was normalized to a0−1scale, and a weighted linear combination was used to calculate the CPI for each model and question as shown in Eq. (2): CP I= 0.3A+ 0.3C+ 0.2E+ 0.2S(2) The weights were selected to emphasize accuracy and completeness (60% combined contribution) as core indi- cators of conceptual and computational correctness, while efficiency and support (40%) capture the response quality and pedagogical richness of the interaction.

DISCUSSION The present study evaluates LLM performance and reason- ing patterns on Bloom-aligned MCQ tasks across multiple engineering domains. It does not measure student learning outcomes or experimentally test instructional interventions. Rather, it analyzes how observed response characteristics may inform the design of future LLM-mediated educational activities. The results illustrate differentiated response patterns among GPT-5, Claude, and Grok when evaluated through a Bloom-aligned assessment structure. Rather than establish- ing inherent cognitive hierarchies among models, the find- ings demonstrate how taxonomy-based analysis can reveal variations in explanation depth, procedural execution, and response structure across engineering domains. Thermodynamics: Quantitative differences also high- lighted model-specific reasoning strategies. In a thermody- namics problem involving temperature-dependent specific heats, Claude correctly reasoned that the difference in values led to only a 0.8% change in energy, accurately noting that this deviation is negligible for small temperature intervals. GPT-5 reached a comparable conclusion but with a 5% numerical error attributable to reference-table rounding, while Grok misapplied constants entirely. Notably, GPT-5 was the only model that cited a credible reference, whereas Claude and Grok refused to identify data sources, indicating limitations in source transparency that affect reproducibility and trustworthiness. GPT-5 initially selected the wrong capacitor value in Question 12, while Claude misidentified the current ratio in the three-phase problem. Grok was accurate throughout but sometimes overanalyzed. Overall, all three models solved the circuit problems effectively. These observations reinforce that generative AI tools must be aligned with learning outcomes and Bloom levels. For lower-order objectives, they can effectively scaffold recall and comprehension. For higher-order objectives,i.e. application, analysis, and evaluation, instructors should de- sign guided prompts that require reasoning steps, anno- tated figures, and explicit justification to prevent superficial correctness. Future work should quantify the impact of such structured prompting on students’ critical thinking and concept retention, expanding analysis across larger item sets and diverse engineering domains. The pedagogical characterizations proposed here (e.g., reflective tutor, accuracy checker) should be understood as design implications inferred from observed response pat- terns rather than experimentally validated instructional roles. V . CONCLUSION This study explored how large language models respond to engineering assessment tasks when analyzed through Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. Within the constraints of the selected courses, item set, and rubric framework, the mod- els demonstrated differentiated performance patterns across cognitive categories. These results should be interpreted as illustrative applications of a structured evaluation approach rather than as generalized claims of expert-level reasoning. For engineering instructors, these findings underscore the need to shift from perceiving AI as a replacement for human cognition to treating it as a cognitive amplifier, a partner that can model reasoning processes, provide immediate formative feedback, and promote metacognitive engagement when used strategically. Instructors should design activities that require students to interrogate AI explanations, identify assumptions, and justify alternative reasoning paths. Embed- ding LLM-assisted exercises into assignments or lab reports can cultivate critical thinking, while structured reflection prompts (e.g., Where might the model’s reasoning fail?) reinforce deeper conceptual understanding. Moreover, LLM output can serve as a benchmark for diagnostic feedback, en- abling educators to identify common student misconceptions and to tailor instruction toward conceptual clarity rather than rote performance.

For students, this work highlights both the potential and the responsibility that accompany AI use in technical learn- ing. When leveraged as an interactive learning companion rather than an answer-generator, LLMs can accelerate com- prehension, offer diverse solution pathways, and support au- tonomous exploration. Yet over-reliance on AI risks eroding the very analytical rigor that defines engineering expertise. Students must therefore approach these tools with skeptical curiosity, validating AI-generated solutions, cross-checking equations, and reflecting on the physical or computational meaning behind every result. Developing such habits will be essential for engineers operating in a future where human- AI collaboration defines professional practice. The findings suggest that Bloom-aligned frameworks may provide a structured lens for analyzing AI-generated responses in educational contexts. Future research should replicate this approach across larger datasets, alternative assessment formats, and diverse institutions to evaluate the stability and transferability of these observations. The present work should be understood as exploratory and methodological in nature. Its primary contribution lies in demonstrating how a taxonomy-aligned analytical frame- work can be applied to interpret LLM responses across engineering domains.
